research_question: Does regular single-byte-XOR beaconing produce a measurably lower timing jitter than ordinary background traffic on a small home network?

related_work.citation: Zeek/Bro NSM project documentation, connection log (conn.log) field reference
related_work.relevance: Defines the connection-record schema this study's own detect_beaconing() logic (Module 14) is modeled on.

related_work.citation: MITRE ATT&CK, T1071 (Application Layer Protocol) and T1568 (Dynamic Resolution)
related_work.relevance: Standard taxonomy for the C2 beaconing behavior class this study measures against, used to frame why timing-jitter is a reasonable detection feature.

methodology.description: Generate synthetic connection logs for both a fixed-interval beaconing process (this module's own beacon_demo, extended to run for 200 iterations) and ordinary background traffic (Module 14's own generate_conn_log.py), compute each dataset's coefficient of variation for inter-connection timing, and compare distributions.
methodology.ethics_statement: All traffic generated and captured is against the researcher's own localhost lab environment only, per this course's SAFETY.md. No third-party systems, networks, or data are involved.

results.summary: Beaconing traffic's timing jitter (coefficient of variation) was consistently below 0.1, while background traffic exceeded 0.5 in all trials -- confirming the jitter-ratio detection principle Module 14 relies on.
results.evidence: 20 trials of 200-connection synthetic logs each, jitter ratios recorded in results/jitter_trials.csv (not included in this sample -- a real study would attach or link the actual dataset).

limitations: All traffic is synthetic, generated by this course's own tools, not observed from a real compromised host -- external validity against real-world malware beaconing behavior is not established by this study alone.
Only single-byte-XOR-obfuscated beaconing was tested; jittered/randomized-interval beaconing (a known evasion technique) was out of scope.
